description: I am Manish, Student Researcher at NIT Warangal.
summary:
ASCLEPIUS is an offline health app for astronauts on long missions, built for the moment when the doctor on Earth can't answer in time. On Mars, a radio message takes up to 22 minutes each way, and in 2028 the Sun blocks the link for 27 days.

Each morning the astronaut spends about a minute entering the six readings in this challenge: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood. Each reading is checked twice, against the normal adult range and against that astronaut's own normal, and the result shows on a body map with the exact rule behind every colour.

For every warning, the Earth Reply Clock uses real NASA JPL Horizons data to work out how long a reply from the flight surgeon would take that day, and tells the crew whether to wait or act now. It also spots patterns across the crew, like shared headaches that point to cabin CO2. Reports to Earth are encrypted and signed, and the flight surgeon can send signed advice back.

I tested the "own normal" idea on real Inspiration4 blood data from NASA OSDR: all four crew changed beyond their own range while still looking normal on the standard one. No AI makes health decisions.
details:
ASCLEPIUS is a health app for astronauts on long missions, built for the moment when the doctor on Earth can't answer in time.

Try it

  • Live app (no login, works offline): https://ibeastmanish.github.io/ASCLEPIUS/
  • Ground Station, the flight surgeon's side (open it in a second tab): https://ibeastmanish.github.io/ASCLEPIUS/ground.html
  • Code, data and tests: https://github.com/ibeastmanish/ASCLEPIUS

A quick path: open the app and look at today's alert and its Earth Reply Clock, then Crew Pulse, then Outbox for the mission forecast. Send the report and it reaches the Ground Station after the real light delay. The flight surgeon can send back signed advice, which takes the same delay to arrive.

What it does

Each morning the astronaut enters six readings: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood. It takes about a minute. Each reading is compared with two things: the normal adult range, and that person's own normal, learned from their first seven checks. The second comparison is the one that matters. A resting heart rate of 74 is fine for most people, but if yours is usually 52 to 62, it's worth a look.

Results show up on a body map in green, yellow or red. Tap any colour and you see the exact rule behind it and where the number comes from. When a few readings point the same way, like poor sleep plus a raised heart rate, the app shows one card ("fatigue pattern") instead of three separate alarms.

What makes it different

Other tools mention the delay to Earth. ASCLEPIUS works it out for the exact mission day and turns it into a decision. On Mars, a radio message takes up to 22 minutes to reach Earth, and the same to come back. So for every warning, the app works out how long a reply from the flight surgeon would really take: the wait for the next contact, the light time each way (from NASA JPL Horizons), and the surgeon's response time. Then it compares that with how soon the crew has to act. For a dangerous low blood sugar on Mars, a reply takes about 27 minutes and the crew has 10. So the app tells them to treat it now and let Earth confirm later.

I ran the same calculation for every day from November 2026 to the end of 2029. That gives the crew a forecast of when they'll be on their own. The longest stretch is 27 days in 2028, when the Sun sits between Earth and Mars and blocks the radio link completely.

It also looks across the whole crew. If one person has a headache, that's about them. If two or three people get headaches on the same day, the cabin air is the more likely cause, so the app checks the CO2 reading against NASA's limit. A fever that shows up in a second person one to three days later is flagged as a possible infection.

There's also a weekly eye check (an Amsler grid and a contrast test), because long missions can change astronauts' eyesight. Each result is compared with that person's earlier ones.

Testing it on real NASA data

I wanted to know if the "your own normal" idea holds up with real astronauts, so I used the Inspiration4 crew blood tests from NASA's OSDR (OSD-569 and OSD-575). After the flight, red blood cell size dropped below each person's own pre-flight range in all four crew members, while all four still looked normal on the standard lab range. While working with the file I found a row whose values were shifted into the wrong columns. I corrected it in my analysis and reported it to the OSDR team.

How it's built

It's an offline web app written in TypeScript and React. It runs on the crew's tablet with no internet and no server, and health data is encrypted on the device. Reports to Earth are signed, encrypted, numbered so they can't be replayed, and padded to the same size, so an emergency message doesn't look different from a routine one. This uses the browser's built-in Web Crypto: AES-256-GCM encryption with a new ECDH P-256 key for every message, ECDSA P-256 signatures, SHA-256 hashing, and PBKDF2 (600,000 rounds) to protect the data on the device. The flight surgeon's private key never touches the crew tablet.

On a real mission they would go from the tablet to the base radio, a relay orbiter, NASA's Deep Space Network and the flight surgeon. In the demo that link is simulated, but the delay is real.

All the health rules live in one readable file, each with its source, and every guidance card names the NASA Human Research Program hazard and risk it relates to. There are 162 automated tests, and I used Python to process the NASA data.

Why it matters beyond space

Near Warangal, where I live, some villages are hours from a doctor. The same idea works there: the app has a clinic mode that uses travel time instead of light time, and the daily check works in Telugu and Hindi.

Limits

This is decision support, not a medical device. The crew data in the demo is simulated and labelled that way. The thresholds would need review by a flight surgeon. The Inspiration4 result comes from four people on a three-day flight, so it supports the idea but doesn't prove it. It hasn't been tested with real users yet; that's the next step.

Use of AI

I used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help research, write and test the code, and draft the documents, slides and video. I checked the health rules and the data analysis myself. The app does not use AI to make health decisions; every alert comes from a written rule with a source. The Telugu and Hindi text is machine-translated and marked as a draft. The demo video voice-over is text-to-speech. No AI-generated images are used.

NASA OSDR OSD-575: Inspiration4 crew Comprehensive Metabolic Panel

OSD-575 data file: LSDS-8 Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CSV)
NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), where we reported the data error
Our corrected OSD-569 blood data (shifted row fixed)
NASA GISS Mars24 Sunclock: Mars time
NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm (used for sol drift)
NASA-STD-3001 Space Flight Human-System Standard, Vol 1 & 2 (NASA Technical Standards)
NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO)
NASA OCHMO-TB-004: Carbon Dioxide technical brief (cabin-air rule)
NASA HRP: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
NASA HRP: Risks of Human Spaceflight
NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge: Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts
NASA image: Blue Marble, Apollo 17 AS17-148-22727

NASA OSDR Biological Data API: OSD-569 dataset
NASA OSDR Biological Data API: OSD-575 dataset
projectRefs: Canadian Space Agency (CSA): Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health

American Diabetes Association Standards of Care (glucose ranges)
AASM/SRS adult sleep duration recommendation (Watson et al. 2015)

LOINC: standard codes for lab and vital-sign readings

Playwright + FFmpeg: demo video recording and editing
